franklin-search-001.description: Complete OCR text of the fullest first-hand narrative of Austin's squadron: the passage of Melville Bay, the finding of Franklin's first winter camp at Beechey Island in August 1850, the winter off Griffith Island and the sledge campaign of spring 1851. Sherard Osborn commanded the steam tender Pioneer under Horatio Thomas Austin and walked the Beechey camp himself on 29 August 1850. The printed page numbers survive in the running heads of the scan.

franklin-search-003.description: Complete OCR text of the second Prince Albert voyage, 1851-52: William Kennedy and Joseph Rene Bellot's winter at Batty Bay, their 1,100-mile sledge journey of spring 1852, and their reaching and naming of Bellot Strait on 7 April 1852. The appendix carries Kennedy's letter to the Admiralty of 9 October 1852.

franklin-search-006.description: Complete OCR text of volume II of Sir Edward Belcher's narrative: the natural history, the appendices, and the official instructions and correspondence, including Belcher's order of 21 April 1854 directing Henry Kellett to leave the Resolute, the private letter that went with it, and Belcher's own defence of the four abandonments. Commander George Henry Richards's journal of the spring of 1853 is printed here in long extract.

franklin-search-013.description: Saved page capture of the Dictionary of Canadian Biography life of William Kennedy, the Red River-born Hudson's Bay Company trader, son of an Orkneyman and a Cree mother, who commanded Lady Franklin's second Prince Albert voyage and who, with Joseph Rene Bellot, reached and named Bellot Strait in April 1852.

franklin-search-017.description: Complete OCR text of volume I of Peter Cormack Sutherland's narrative of William Penny's expedition, written by the surgeon of the brig Sophia: the passage out, the finding of Franklin's first winter camp at Beechey Island in August 1850, and the settling of the two brigs into Assistance Bay for the winter. The scan is a UCLA copy and its OCR is rough; spellings should be checked against the page images before quoting.

franklin-search-018.description: Complete OCR text of volume II of Peter Cormack Sutherland's narrative: the winter at Assistance Bay, the sledge and boat journeys of spring 1851 including William Penny's finding of open water at the head of Wellington Channel in May, the appendices, and Penny's side of his quarrel with Horatio Thomas Austin.

franklin-search-023.description: Most of this track is measured rather than inferred: George Frederick M'Dougall was the Resolute's master, and his appendix prints a table of positions (pp. 481-486) and a day-by-day drift table for the autumn of 1853 (pp. 359-360). Waypoints marked as stated are his observed latitudes and longitudes. The line runs from Greenhithe in April 1852 to Beechey Island in August, west along Barrow Strait to within six miles of Parry's Winter Harbour, and into winter quarters off Dealy Island, from which Henry Kellett's sledge parties reached the Investigator in the spring of 1853. The ship was blown out of Bridport Inlet in August 1853, beset again a month later, and drifted 180 miles east in the pack before freezing in for a second winter twenty-eight miles south-west of Cape Cockburn. Sir Edward Belcher ordered her abandoned there on 15 May 1854, in latitude 74 deg 41 min 30 sec N, longitude 101 deg 22 min W. Sixteen months later she was found derelict in Davis Strait, more than a thousand miles away, by the American whaling master James Buddington; the last leg of this line, from May 1854 to September 1855, is a straight line between two points and represents no observed track at all. The United States bought her, refitted her and gave her back to Britain in 1856. When she was broken up, timber from her hull was made into the desk that has stood in the Oval Office ever since.

franklin-search-025.description: Lady Franklin's first ship: a ninety-ton fruit ketch bought out of the Azores trade, strengthened at Aberdeen, and sent north in June 1850 under Commander Charles Codrington Forsyth with a crew of eighteen and about 1,500 pounds of public subscription behind her. William Parker Snow, Lady Franklin's man aboard, gives about a dozen genuine noon positions, marked here as stated; the rest are the places he names. Her orders were to search the west coast of Prince Regent Inlet down to the Gulf of Boothia - which is to say, almost exactly the right ground - but she was stopped by ice off Fury Beach on 23 August and Forsyth turned for home the same afternoon over Snow's objection. On the way out she called at Cape Riley on 25 August, where Snow copied Erasmus Ommanney's notice, and so the Prince Albert carried the news of the first traces of Franklin home to England in October 1850, a year before the naval squadron came back.

franklin-search-028.description: Complete OCR text of Francis Leopold McClintock's narrative of the voyage that closed the search: the 242-day drift in the Baffin Bay pack, the second start of 1858, the passage of Bellot Strait at the fifth attempt on 6 September 1858, the winter at Port Kennedy, the sledge journeys of spring 1859 and the record William Hobson found at Victory Point.

franklin-search-030.description: The first announcement of the first trace of Franklin, left by Erasmus Ommanney in a cairn at the foot of Cape Riley and copied out two days later by William Parker Snow, who landed there from the Prince Albert. It is the only contemporary document of the find printed in any of the 1850 narratives: 'This is to certify that Captain Ommanney, with the officers of her Majesty's ships Assistance and Intrepid, landed at Cape Riley on the 23rd of August, 1850, where he found traces of an encampment, and collected the remains of materials which evidently prove that some party belonging to her Majesty's ships have been detained on this spot. Beechey Island was also examined, where traces were found of the same party.' Note what it does not say: no record, no document, no indication of where the party went.

franklin-search-057.description: The pamphlet in which John Rae's despatch of 29 July 1854 from Repulse Bay was published, together with the despatches of Robert McClure and other officers. It carries the report of what Inuit told Rae at Pelly Bay and at Naujaat about the forty white men who starved near the Back River, and the sentence about cannibalism that cost Rae his reputation in Britain.

franklin-search-060.title: M'Dougall's table of coast searched and newly charted, 1848-1854
franklin-search-060.description: The search's own accounting of what it had put on the chart, printed in the appendix to George Frederick M'Dougall's narrative of the Resolute under the heading 'Land discovered and searched from 1848 to 1854'. Geographical miles first, statute miles second. Sir James Clark Ross 1848-49: 990/1,143 searched on foot, 200/230 of coast newly charted. Horatio Thomas Austin 1850-51: 6,087/7,025 searched, 1,076/1,225 new. William Penny 1850-51: 1,700/1,965 searched, 500/578 new (measured, M'Dougall notes, from Belcher's corrected chart of Wellington Channel). Robert McClure 1850-53: 2,350/2,710 searched, 1,591/1,838 new. John Rae 1851: 1,030/1,190 searched, 617/712 new. Edward Augustus Inglefield 1852: 180/208 new, taken from the vessel with no travelling at all. Henry Kellett 1852-54: 9,432/10,881 searched on foot - excluding the march to Beechey Island after the ship was abandoned - and 1,618/1,870 new. Totals: 21,589 geographical (24,914 statute) miles searched on foot, and 5,782 geographical (6,661 statute) miles of coast laid down for the first time. A second table on the same sheet breaks the 1,618 miles down by party: M'Clintock 768 geographical miles, Mecham 680, Hamilton 170, all of it in the spring of 1853. Sir Edward Belcher's own division is missing from the table, and no aggregate for it appears in his volume I.

franklin-search-069.description: Complete OCR text of the parliamentary paper in which the Admiralty's Arctic Committee examined whether Horatio Thomas Austin's and William Penny's expeditions had searched Wellington Channel properly in 1850-51: lix plus 199 pages of minutes of evidence from the officers of both squadrons and of Sir John Ross's Felix, together with the official instructions to Edwin Jesse De Haven and to Saunders of the North Star, and reports of Inuit testimony. Austin's own official narrative of his voyage, printed at the front, is the authority for the casualties of the 1851 sledge campaign and for the death of George S. Malcolm.

franklin-search-076.description: Austin's four ships - Resolute, Assistance, and the steam tenders Intrepid and Pioneer - housed over on the fixed floe between Griffith Island and Cape Martyr through the winter of 1850-51, attributed to William Henry James Browne, a naval officer who had wintered with James Clark Ross at Port Leopold in 1848-49 and drew several of the best-known views of the search. Horatio Thomas Austin commanded the squadron, Erasmus Ommanney the Assistance and Sherard Osborn the Pioneer; Francis Leopold McClintock was one of the lieutenants. Only a small 512 by 301 pixel reproduction survives in the public file, taken from a saleroom photograph rather than an institutional scan; a larger copy would have to come from the Royal Museums Greenwich or from the original sale catalogue.

franklin-search-079.description: Complete OCR text of volume II of the English edition of Joseph Rene Bellot's memoirs: his own day-by-day journal from October 1851 through the winter at Batty Bay and the sledge journey of February to May 1852, including his own account of the days at Brentford Bay when he and William Kennedy walked the channel that Kennedy named after him. Bellot's journal of 6 and 7 April 1852 (pp. 174-176) shows that he did not understand at the time that he had found a strait: he took the water for a lake, and the sun told him it lay to the south rather than to the west.

franklin-search-080.description: Complete OCR text of volume II of John Richardson's narrative: the winter of 1848-49 at Fort Confidence on Great Bear Lake, the instructions of 1 May 1849 handing the search over to John Rae, Rae's failed crossing to Wollaston Land in August 1849, and Richardson's return to Liverpool on 6 November 1849 after nineteen months. It also carries the long appendix on the physical geography of northern America. Volume I stops at the arrival at Fort Confidence on 15 September 1848.

franklin-search-081.description: Not a report but a single large printed broadside, a table 'compiled from official Documents, and respectfully inscribed to his Captain, by George F. M'Dougall, Master of H.M.S. Resolute'. Every sledge journey of the spring of 1853 has a row: the names and rank of the whole party including the men, the sledge's flag and motto (Beauty, Perseverance, Hope, Star of the North, John Barrow, Murchison, Frazer), the written order it carried, the dates of leaving and of return, hours travelling and encamped, the furthest position attained with its latitude, longitude and date, geographical and statute miles, game procured, meteorology, and a column of remarks. Despite the second title line naming Sir Edward Belcher, the sheet covers only Henry Kellett's western branch, the parties from the Resolute and Intrepid at Dealy Island - Bedford Pim, Domville, Roche, Francis Leopold McClintock, George Frederick Mecham, Richard Vesey Hamilton, George Nares, Emile de Bray, M'Dougall and W. H. Richards. It carries nothing on Belcher's eastern division. The force it accounts for is 84 officers and men and 10 dogs. The one item touching the eastern division is the remark that Lieutenant Hamilton 'fell in with Commander Richards of H.M. Ship Assistance, on the 18th May, about 6 miles S.E. of Cape Richards' - the only contact between Belcher's and Kellett's divisions in two years.

franklin-search-095.description: The one man Austin's squadron lost in two years, and the settling of a disagreement between two of the printed narratives. Sherard Osborn's book calls him 'John Malcolm, a seaman'; Peter Cormack Sutherland calls him George Malcolm, captain of the hold. Horatio Thomas Austin's own official narrative, printed in the 1852 blue book, is decisive: 'They brought in casualties of men, wholly from frostbite, to the number of eighteen; one of which (it is my painful duty to relate) ended fatally. George S. Malcolm, captain of the hold of the Resolute, a native of Dundee, whose death was attributed to exhaustion and frostbite brought on whilst labouring as captain of the sledge Excellent, (virtually, it may be said,) died at his post.' He was buried on the north-east shore of Griffith Island.

franklin-search-116.description: The complete scan of Francis Leopold McClintock's narrative of the Fox, the private expedition Lady Franklin paid for, which found the Victory Point record and settled the fate of Franklin's people. The plates and maps shown separately here - the two front sketch maps, the frontispiece, and the wood engravings after Captain May, Allen Young and others - are all cut from this copy.
